items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: A thrown ball at 10 m/s reaches the same height regardless of angle
items.claim: Throw a ball straight up at 10 m/s: it reaches 5.1 metres. Throw it at 45 degrees with horizontal speed component 7.07 m/s and vertical 7.07 m/s: the vertical component alone determines max height (2.55 m). The horizontal speed is irrelevant to height.
items.prompt: Why doesn't horizontal velocity affect maximum height?

options.text: Horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT (Galileo's insight). Gravity only acts vertically; horizontal velocity remains constant (in vacuum) and contributes nothing to vertical position. Maximum height depends only on initial vertical velocity component
Horizontal motion adds to height through Pythagoras

items.reveal:
Galileo's insight (~1604): motion can be decomposed into independent perpendicular components. Vertical motion under gravity proceeds the same way regardless of horizontal motion.

For a projectile launched at speed v at angle theta above horizontal:
- Horizontal velocity: v * cos(theta), constant in vacuum.
- Vertical velocity: v * sin(theta) initially, decreasing under gravity.
- Max height: h = (v * sin(theta))^2 / (2g). Independent of horizontal component.
- Range (in vacuum): R = v^2 * sin(2 * theta) / g.
- Time aloft: t = 2 * v * sin(theta) / g.

Dropping a bullet and firing it horizontally simultaneously: they hit the ground at the same time (assuming flat ground, no air resistance). The horizontal motion of the fired bullet doesn't change its vertical fall. This was first demonstrated experimentally by Galileo's student Vincenzo Viviani.

Mythbusters tested this with .45 caliber bullets (S07E11): bullet dropped vs bullet fired horizontally landed almost simultaneously (with millisecond-scale differences from air, recoil, ground curvature).

Applications:
- Artillery: vertical and horizontal trajectories computed separately, then composed.
- Skydiving: horizontal travel during fall depends on jump speed; vertical fall time depends only on altitude.
- Sports: free throws, basketball shots, soccer kicks — coaches train the vertical component for height and arc, horizontal for distance.

With air resistance, the decomposition is not exact — drag depends on total velocity, mixing the components. But the vacuum result is the framework.
items.why: Motion in two directions seems like it should interact. Galileo's discovery that perpendicular motions are independent is one of the deepest simplifications in physics — and the reason projectile problems are solvable at all.

items.title: A shape with finite volume but infinite surface area
items.claim: Rotate y = 1/x for x at least 1 around the x-axis. You get a 'horn' extending to infinity. Its volume is exactly pi (finite). Its surface area is infinite. You could fill it with paint, but never paint its interior.
items.prompt: How can volume be finite if surface area isn't?

options.text: The horn cannot be constructed in reality
Volume integrates 1/x squared (which is summable), while surface integrates 1/x (which is not); the integrals are independent, and one can converge while the other diverges
Surface and volume are always proportional in finite shapes

items.reveal:
Volume: V = pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) squared dx = pi * [-1/x] from 1 to infinity = pi.

Surface area: A = 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) * sqrt(1 + 1/x to the fourth) dx, which is greater than 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x = infinity.

Intuition: volume scales as the square of the radius, surface as the radius. As you stretch toward infinity, the cross-sectional radius decreases as 1/x — the square (volume per unit length) decreases as 1/x squared (summable), but the radius itself (surface per unit length) decreases as 1/x (the harmonic series, divergent).

The 'paint paradox': filling the horn with pi cubic units of paint coats the interior — even though the surface 'should' need infinite paint to cover. The resolution: a paint film of any finite thickness doesn't fit at the horn's far reaches, where the radius is arbitrarily small.
items.why: Geometric intuition equates surface area and volume scaling. They're separate integrals; convergence of one doesn't imply convergence of the other.
